stops.name: Santiago, the Escuela Normal de Preceptores
stops.campa: Manuel Montt, minister of instruction, gives the stateless journalist a state: the first teacher-training school in South America, and Sarmiento as its founding director. Twenty-eight students, a curriculum he writes himself, a manual for country schoolteachers, and a principle that will govern the rest of his life — that you do not make schools by building rooms, you make them by manufacturing teachers, and that this is a task of industrial scale. Everything from Paraná in 1870 to the kindergarten of 1884 descends from this room in Santiago.

stops.name: Santiago, the Memoria sobre ortografía americana
stops.campa: Before the Faculty of Humanities of the University of Chile, the man who learned to read from his mother proposes to reform the spelling of the Spanish language on American ground: one letter, one sound; abolish what the ear does not hear. Andrés Bello, the greatest grammarian in the hemisphere, receives him with courtesy and partial assent. Chile adopts a version of the reform and keeps it for decades. Sarmiento never fully abandons it — his own books print i for y, and the title page of the Viajes still says Africa i America.

stops.name: Santiago, Facundo appears in the folletín of El Progreso
stops.campa: In serial instalments at the foot of a Santiago newspaper, and then as a book, appears Civilización i barbarie: vida de Juan Facundo Quiroga. It is biography, geography, polemic, prophecy and libel at once, written at speed to wreck a diplomatic mission of Rosas. It invents the Argentine literary tradition by accident. Its first move is to read the pampa as Asia: the ox-cart train as a camel caravan bound for Baghdad, the wagon-master as a caravan chief, the mounted raiders as Bedouin. The desert is the key, and the key is borrowed from the Orient.
stops.quote: Hay algo en las soledades argentinas que trae a la memoria las soledades asiáticas; alguna analogía encuentra el espíritu entre la pampa y las llanuras que median entre el Tigris y el Eúfrates.
stops.quote_source: Facundo, cap. I, 'Aspecto físico de la República Argentina' (1845)

stops.name: Santiago, the gaucho written as a Bedouin
stops.campa: The analogy hardens into a system. The tribe on the Asian steppe is the estancia; the caudillo is a Mahoma who could change the religion at will; the montonera that destroyed the cities of the interior is exactly the Bedouin horde now harrying the frontiers of French Algeria — same war, same men, same undisciplined strategy. He has never seen Africa. He is writing from a newspaper office in Santiago, out of Volney and the reviews, and he says so plainly. Within eighteen months he will be standing in that country, checking his own metaphor against the ground.
stops.quote: Las hordas beduinas que hoy importunan con su algazara y depredaciones las fronteras de la Argelia dan una idea exacta de la montonera argentina... La misma lucha de civilización y barbarie, de la ciudad y el desierto, existe hoy en África.

stops.name: Valparaíso, embarkation on the government's commission
stops.campa: Chile is embarrassed by him and cannot spare him, so it sends him away usefully: a commission from Montt to inspect at first hand the primary-school systems of Europe and North America, funded by the state, with the rank of an official traveller. He sails at the end of October with letters of introduction and a plan to see everything. He is thirty-four, has never left the Southern Cone, and will be gone two and a half years. The letters he writes home become the Viajes por Europa, África i América.

stops.name: Montevideo, the besieged city
stops.campa: The first letter of the Viajes is dated from a city under siege. Montevideo has been invested by Oribe and Rosas for three years and is held by a garrison of French, Italian and Argentine exiles; Garibaldi is in the harbour, the Argentine emigration is in the cafés, and Facundo is being read there before its author arrives. He finds his own reputation waiting for him on the wharf. The exile discovers that a book travels faster than a man, and that he has become, without a country, a public person.

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the slave empire
stops.campa: From the letter dated Rio, February 1846: a tropical capital of extraordinary beauty resting on a population of enslaved Africans, an emperor of twenty in a court of European manners, and a whole society that strikes him as a machine running on a fuel he considers morally and economically ruinous. He counts the numbers, as he always does. Brazil is his first sight of a plantation order at scale, and it sharpens the argument he will make for the rest of his life: that a country is made or unmade by the composition of its people.

stops.name: Grand Bourg, a day alone with San Martín
stops.campa: An hour outside Paris, in a modest house by the Seine, lives the man who crossed the Andes, forgotten by the countries he made. Sarmiento is brought in by old friends' letters and given a whole day. He touches certain strings on purpose — a portrait of Bolívar noticed by chance — and watches the countryman of Grand Bourg vanish and the young general reappear, the bent back straightening, the small clouded eyes opening. Then they name Rosas, and the vision collapses: the old man defends the tyrant as the defender of American independence.
stops.quote: He pasado con él momentos sublimes, que quedarán para siempre grabados en mi espíritu. Solos un día entero... lo he visto transfigurarse, i desaparecer a mi vista el campagnard de Grandbourg i presentárseme el jeneral joven, que asoma sobre las cúspides de los Andes.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta a Antonino Aberastain, París, 4 de septiembre de 1846

stops.name: Paris, the cunas and the salles d'asile
stops.campa: The commission is discharged on foot, school by school. A patroness of the Faubourg Saint-Germain, Madame Gresier, dresses down to the plainness of the nurses so as not to shame them, and guides him through the crèches and the infant asylums of Paris: hundreds of children in a yard, women in charge, reading and counting and singing and gymnastics before the age of six. He writes it all up for De la educación popular. This, not Froebel, is the first model of early schooling he carries back across the Atlantic.
stops.quote: Las Salas de Asilo, la más bella, la más útil y la más fecunda en resultados morales de todas las instituciones modernas.

stops.name: Madrid, the reckoning with the mother country
stops.campa: The long letter to Lastarria from Madrid is the most brutal thing in the Viajes: a Spanish America settling accounts with Spain. He goes to the Teatro del Príncipe, sits in Romea's dressing room, and reports that in a week a foreigner can meet, and be on familiar terms with, every literary reputation in the country. Spain has produced no Byron, no Goethe, no Lamartine; the octosyllable of blind beggars is its measure. The bullfight appalls and fascinates him. He leaves convinced that the inheritance he must escape is Spanish.
stops.quote: Basta conocer un poco a Madrid para medir el alcance del drama español. Madrid, aunque real i mui noble, es siempre la villa de Madrid.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta a Victorino Lastarria, Madrid, 15 de noviembre de 1846

stops.name: Orán, the letter from Africa begins
stops.campa: He has left Spain carrying letters to Marshal Bugeaud and a near-order to a consul to put him aboard the first warship going over. The African letter of the Viajes opens at Orán on the second of January, seventeen years into the French conquest and eleven months before the emir's surrender. This is a war zone, and he has arrived as an official guest of the army waging it. He is the only Latin American writer of his generation to walk into the Algerian war on purpose, to check a metaphor.
stops.quote: Ahora parto para África. Llevo cartas para el Mariscal Bugeaud, i una casi orden al Cónsul de Mallorca, para que me haga conducir a Arjel por el primer vapor de guerra que se presente.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta desde España, vísperas del paso a África (1846)

stops.name: The plain of the Mitidja, the colony and the fever
stops.campa: Behind Algiers spreads the Mitidja, the showpiece of French colonisation: Roman-looking roads, handsome new buildings, an apparent Europe transplanted. He is not fooled for a paragraph. Under the marsh lies malaria; the torrents off the Atlas erase a decade's work in an hour; a village of eight hundred has just been drowned overnight. And under the colony lies the country, unconverted. He is the same writer here as at home: the surface is civilisation, the substrate is the desert, and the substrate is patient.
stops.quote: El velado horizonte árabe está ahí siempre, i bajo sus anchos pliegues, un pueblo orijinal, un idioma primitivo, i una relijion intolerante... La tristeza habitual del grave semblante árabe está revelando, en su humildad aparente, ... la enerjia que no se somete, sino que aplaza para días mejores la venganza.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta desde África (Orán–Argel, enero de 1847)
